chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: High concern (differential post-survey exclusion): Of 288 targeted households, 274 questionnaires were completed (all 14 non-respondents were in formal communities), and 62 of 274 completed questionnaires (22.6%) were excluded from analysis—predominantly due to the requirement of continuous residence since 1998—with severe differential exclusion in informal settlements (52/138 [37.7%] dropped) versus formal settlements (10/136 [7.4%] dropped) (PDF pp. 11–13, Table 3).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: No unprivatised comparison municipality or control group exists, and no multivariable regression or quasi-experimental adjustment was performed to separate the 1998 privatisation from 1998–2003 post-Asian-financial-crisis macroeconomic recovery, municipal groundwater/land-subsidence policies, or household-level covariates (PDF pp. 8, 14–15).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate (institutional level) / Weak (household tenure level): The institutional terms of the 25-year BOOT concession between PWA and PTW (tariff control, bulk water purchase rates, unbundled maintenance contracts, and water-loss targets) are well documented from official PWA sources (Section 3, Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10). However, household legal tenure was not directly measured via land titles or deeds; instead, tenure informality was proxied ecologically at the settlement level via the National Housing Authority (NHA) 2000 slum (Chum Chon) classification, even though the authors acknowledge some informal-settlement households may have held legal tenure (PDF pp. 12, 17, 25 n. 11).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Although 2003 piped water connections and monthly bills were verified by inspecting meters and latest bills, all 1998 pre-privatisation household-level baselines (connection status, water quality, service quality, connection cost, and monthly bill) relied on 5-year retrospective recall in 2003, household water/service quality attributes were coarse binary perceptions, and 2003 household income was applied retroactively to classify 1998 poverty status (PDF pp. 13–14).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-low quality: Current (2003) piped dwelling connections and monthly bills were objectively checked on site (PDF p. 14), and municipal-wide water quality/service metrics (Pt-Co, NTU, pH, TDS, E. coli, pressure in bars, complaint response minutes) were compiled from PWA technical reports (Table 6, PDF p. 21). However, all household-level pre-post change measures relied on 5-year retrospective recall of 1998 baselines and subjective binary quality perceptions, while PWA laboratory reports were single municipal-wide observations not disaggregated by poor or informal communities (and post-privatisation report C 154/46 was dated November 2002 despite being labelled 2003/2004; PDF pp. 11, 21–22).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No study protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported (No information on pre-registration). Willingness-to-pay survey findings are summarized selectively in Endnote 18 without tabular reporting (PDF p. 26), and statistically insignificant chi-squared tests in small subsamples (n=38 to n=86) are interpreted as validating Proposition 3 (no cost increase for a large portion of the poor) despite 16–32 percentage-point increases in households paying higher connection fees and monthly bills (PDF p. 18, Table 4).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Pathumthani was purposively chosen by the Thai government as the first water privatisation site due to its financial attractiveness and proximity to Bangkok (PDF pp. 8, 24 n. 4). Within Amphoe Muang, the first-stage selection method for choosing 5 of 18 informal and 5 of 12 formal communities is not specified as random, and restricting analysis to households residing at the same address since at least 1998 excluded mobile/recent slum migrants and disproportionately removed 37.7% of interviewed informal-community households (PDF pp. 11–13, Table 3).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Inclusion criteria were clearly stated: households had to reside within the 10 sampled communities (5 informal, 5 formal) in the urban district (Amphoe Muang) of Pathumthani province, respondents were household heads or knowledgeable adult members regardless of ownership or tenancy status, and households had to have lived in the location continuously since at least 1998 to report pre-privatisation conditions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The institutional context of the 1998 Pathumthani BOOT water concession (Section 3, Table 1), the demographic and physical profile of Amphoe Muang (population, household size, census tenure and baseline service shares, manufacturing base; Section 4.2), and the stratified community and income groups (small vs. large NHA-classified informal settlements, planned estates, shop-houses, single dwellings, and income-poor vs. non-poor households; Section 4.3, Table 3) are described in detail.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Exposure to privatisation was uniform across the entire study district (no unexposed comparator municipality), with pre/post status defined temporally (1998 vs. 2003). For cross-group poverty/tenure comparisons, settlement informality relied on an ecological 2000 NHA slum classification rather than household-level tenure verification, and household income poverty (<=7,500 baht/month) was self-reported in 2003 and applied retroactively to 1998 without measuring baseline 1998 income.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Standard institutional criteria were used to classify informal slum communities (National Housing Authority 2000 Chum Chon classification and the <=200 vs. >200 household size cut-off), household poverty (Bank of Thailand <=7,500 baht/month threshold benchmarked against NESDB poverty lines), and municipal technical water quality standards (WHO/PWA permissible limits in Table 6).

Beyond descriptive stratification by community informality, settlement size, and 2003 household income, the authors did not identify key time-varying confounders between 1998 and 2003 (e.g., macroeconomic recovery following Thailand's 1997 financial crisis, general urban growth in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region, groundwater land-subsidence regulations, or household income mobility) or household-level covariates (e.g., owner vs. renter status within slums, household size, distance to mains).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No analytical or design strategies to control for confounding—such as an unprivatised control municipality, difference-in-differences estimation, matching, or multivariable regression—were stated or implemented; analyses were restricted to unadjusted bivariate percentage changes within strata.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Although 2003 piped water connections and monthly bills were verified on site via physical inspection of meters/pipes and latest bills, all 1998 baseline household outcomes (access, water quality, service quality, connection cost, and monthly bill) relied on 5-year retrospective recall in 2003, and household water/service quality outcomes were subjective binary perceptions. Supplementary PWA laboratory and operational figures were single municipal-wide observations not disaggregated by community or income group (and post-privatisation water quality report C 154/46 was dated November 2002).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4.1, Table 2, Section 4.4, Section 5.3, Tables 6–7 (PDF pp. 10–11, 14, 21–22)

domain_ratings.justification: Within-household pre-post changes between 1998 and 2003 on the same 212 retained households were tested using independent-sample chi-squared statistics rather than paired tests (e.g., McNemar's test), clustering across the 10 sampled communities in the two-stage sample was ignored, no multivariable models or confidence intervals were reported, and statistical non-significance in small subsamples (designed with 10% margin of error at 90% confidence) was misinterpreted as evidence of no cost increase.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4.3, Section 4.5, Tables 4–5, Section 5.1, Note 13 (PDF pp. 12–20, 25)

overall_narrative_summary: High concern. Zaki and Amin (2009) conducted a single-site 2003 stratified cross-sectional household survey (288 targeted, 274 completed, 212 analysed) in Amphoe Muang, Pathumthani province, Thailand, asking households to recall their pre-privatisation (1998) water supply conditions alongside current (2003) conditions and comparing informal versus formal settlements and income-poor versus non-poor subgroups, supplemented by aggregate Provincial Waterworks Authority (PWA) operational and water-quality records. While the paper provides valuable institutional documentation of Thailand's unbundled BOOT concession structure (where PWA retained retail tariff setting and billing) and verified 2003 household connections and monthly bills directly, it has major methodological limitations for causal or comparative inference: (1) there is no unprivatised comparison municipality to separate the 1998 concession from post-1997 Asian financial crisis recovery and secular urban infrastructure growth; (2) all 1998 household baseline measures relied on 5-year retrospective recall in 2003 and subjective binary perceptions of water/service quality; (3) restricting the analytic sample to households continuously resident since 1998 excluded mobile slum residents and dropped 37.7% (52/138) of interviewed informal-settlement households versus 7.4% (10/136) in formal settlements; (4) household legal tenure was proxied ecologically at the community level rather than measured directly, and 2003 income was applied retroactively to 1998; and (5) statistical testing relied on unadjusted, unpaired, unclustered chi-squared tests across bivariate contingency tables.
study_design_identified: Single-site stratified cross-sectional household survey (conducted in 2003, n=212 analysed) with 5-year retrospective recall of pre-privatisation (1998) conditions and bivariate subgroup comparisons across community tenure/size and income strata, supplemented by aggregate municipal utility records (no unprivatised control arm)
where_found_summary: Section 3 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 8–10) for institutional/contractual exposure details; Section 4.1–4.5 and Tables 2–3 (PDF pp. 10–15) and Endnotes 10–17 (PDF pp. 25–26) for sampling, inclusion criteria, questionnaire recall design, poverty/informality thresholds, and chi-squared analysis; Section 5.1–5.3 and Tables 4–7 (PDF pp. 15–23) and Endnote 18 (PDF p. 26) for empirical results and PWA technical data comparisons.
why_tool_chosen: All sampled households were drawn from a single privatised municipal district (Amphoe Muang, Pathumthani) with no non-privatised comparator utility or quasi-experimental counterfactual design (ruling out ROBINS-I under review rules prohibiting single-case/no-comparator assignment to ROBINS-I). Empirically, the primary dataset is a single 2003 cross-sectional stratified household survey comparing analytical subgroups (informal vs. formal communities, small vs. large informal settlements, and income-poor vs. non-poor households) on current (2003) and retrospectively recalled (1998) water access, quality, and cost indicators; therefore, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the closest matching formal appraisal instrument.
